title: Transformers & Activations
blurb: Reason about softmax invariants, attention shape bookkeeping, and activation failure modes — the math behind every transformer.

cells.title: Softmax: probabilities from logits
cells.body:
Softmax turns a vector of arbitrary real numbers (logits) into a probability distribution: p_i = exp(z_i) / Σ exp(z_j). Three properties always hold, and each one is a debugging tool. Every output is positive (an exponential is never zero). The outputs sum to 1 whatever the logits are — there is no normalization prerequisite. And softmax is invariant to adding a constant to every logit: exp(z_i + c) = exp(c)·exp(z_i), and the exp(c) factor cancels between numerator and denominator.

That shift invariance is why every serious implementation computes exp(z − max(z)): subtracting the largest logit prevents overflow while leaving the result mathematically identical. It also explains a modeling fact: only the differences between logits matter, never their absolute level.

demo.code:
import math

def softmax(z):
    e = [math.exp(v) for v in z]
    total = sum(e)
    return [v / total for v in e]

p = softmax([0.0, 1.0, 2.0])
print('probs:', [round(v, 4) for v in p])
print('sum:', round(sum(p), 6), ' all positive:', all(v > 0 for v in p))

shifted = softmax([5.0, 6.0, 7.0])       # every logit + 5
print('after +5 shift, differences:',
      [abs(a - b) < 1e-12 for a, b in zip(p, shifted)])

cells.title: Attention is three projections and one recipe
cells.body:
Self-attention in one recipe, shapes only. Each token's representation is projected three ways — queries Q, keys K and values V, each of shape (batch, T, d). Scores are Q @ K with K transposed — shape (batch, T, T) — where entry (i, j) asks 'how much does query i match key j?'. A softmax over the last axis (across the keys) turns each query's row into weights summing to 1. Multiplying by V contracts the key axis: (batch, T, T) @ (batch, T, d) = (batch, T, d) — each output token is a weighted average of value vectors.

Two invariants to carry in your head: the score matrix is always T × T (tokens attend to tokens — the feature dimension is what gets contracted away), and the softmax runs per query row, because each query must distribute a total budget of 1 across the keys. Real attention adds only one thing to this picture: scores are divided by sqrt(d) before the softmax, which changes values, never shapes.

demo.code:
import math

def softmax(z):
    e = [math.exp(v) for v in z]
    s = sum(e)
    return [v / s for v in e]

Q = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]]      # 2 tokens, 2 dims
K = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]]
V = [[10.0, 0.0], [0.0, 10.0]]

scores = [[sum(qi * kj for qi, kj in zip(qrow, krow))
           for krow in K] for qrow in Q]
print('scores:', len(scores), 'x', len(scores[0]), ' (queries x keys)')
weights = [softmax(row) for row in scores]      # each ROW sums to 1
print('row sums:', [round(sum(r), 4) for r in weights])
context = [[sum(w * v for w, v in zip(wrow, vrow))
            for vrow in V] for wrow in weights]
print('context:', len(context), 'x', len(context[0]), ' (tokens x dims)')
print('token 0 output:', [round(v, 3) for v in context[0]])

cells.title: Activation ranges and their failure modes
cells.body:
Activation functions are chosen for their ranges and slopes, because backpropagation multiplies slopes along the chain. Sigmoid squashes into (0, 1) with slope s·(1 − s) — at most 0.25 (at z = 0, where s = 0.5) and nearly 0 once the output saturates near 0.0 or 1.0. Stack several sigmoid layers and even the best case multiplies small factors (0.25³ ≈ 0.016); with saturated units, the gradient reaching early layers collapses — the vanishing gradient problem.

ReLU outputs max(0, z): range [0, ∞), slope exactly 1 for positive inputs and exactly 0 for negative ones. Its failure mode is different: a unit whose pre-activation is negative for every sample outputs 0 and passes zero gradient through every path — its weights freeze. That is a dead neuron, diagnosed by outputs stuck at exactly 0.0 for all samples, not merely by zeros appearing sometimes.

exercise.title: Predict: which softmax statement is true
exercise.statement: First, the math every transformer sits on. The snippet computes the same softmax twice — once on small logits, once on the same logits with 50 added to every one — and prints a comparison. Read it, run it in your head, and decide which statement about softmax is TRUE.
exercise.code:
import numpy as np

def softmax(z):
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=float)
    e = np.exp(z - z.max())      # the classic stability shift
    return e / e.sum()

p1 = softmax([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])
p2 = softmax([52.0, 51.0, 50.1])   # every logit + 50
print(p1)
print(p1.sum())
print(np.allclose(p1, p2))
options: A. Every output is positive, the three outputs sum to 1, and p1 equals p2 (up to float rounding): adding 50 to every logit changes nothing.
B. The outputs sum to 1, but p2 differs from p1 — adding 50 to every logit stretches the largest probability further away from the others.
C. The largest logit always receives probability exactly 1.0; the other two receive 0.0.
D. The outputs sum to 1 only because all three logits here are positive; with negative logits, softmax needs renormalization first.
exercise.explain: Compute it: e² ≈ 7.389, e¹ ≈ 2.718, e^0.1 ≈ 1.105, total ≈ 11.213, so p1 ≈ [0.659, 0.242, 0.099] — all positive, summing to 1. Now add 50 to every logit: each exponential grows by a factor of e^50, but that same factor appears in every numerator and in the denominator, so it cancels — softmax(z + c) = softmax(z). That is why the printed allclose is True, and it is exactly why the stability trick z − z.max() inside the function is legal: subtracting a constant is free. B misses the cancellation; C confuses softmax with argmax — the top logit gets 7.389/11.213 ≈ 0.66, and softmax only approaches a one-hot as the gaps grow toward infinity ('soft' is the whole point); D invents a non-negativity requirement — logits may be any real numbers, and the sum is 1 regardless.

exercise.title: Predict: attention shapes
exercise.statement: Attention is mostly shape bookkeeping — if you can multiply matrices in your head, you can read any attention implementation. Predict the shapes of scores and context, and the axis the softmax normalizes over.
exercise.code:
import numpy as np

def softmax_lastaxis(a):
    e = np.exp(a - a.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

batch, T, d = 2, 5, 16
Q = np.random.rand(batch, T, d)
K = np.random.rand(batch, T, d)
V = np.random.rand(batch, T, d)

scores  = Q @ K.transpose(0, 2, 1)    # (batch, ?, ?)
weights = softmax_lastaxis(scores)    # softmax over which axis?
context = weights @ V                 # (batch, ?, ?)
print(scores.shape, context.shape)
options: A. scores (2, 16, 16); softmax over the last axis; context (2, 16, 16)
B. scores (2, 5, 5); softmax over the first of the two matrix axes (each key's column across the 5 queries); context (2, 5, 16)
C. scores (2, 5, 5); softmax over the last axis; context (2, 5, 5)
D. scores (2, 5, 5); softmax over the last axis (each query's row across the 5 keys); context (2, 5, 16)
exercise.explain: K.transpose(0, 2, 1) has shape (2, 16, 5); the batched matmul contracts Q's last axis (16) against K-transposed's last axis (16), leaving the two 5s: scores = (2, 5, 5). Entry [b, i, j] measures how much query i attends to key j. The softmax must normalize over j — the last axis — so each query's row of weights sums to 1 and can act as a mixing distribution over the values. Finally weights @ V: (2, 5, 5) @ (2, 5, 16) contracts the key axis (5) against V's rows, producing (2, 5, 16) — for each token, one 16-dimensional weighted average of value vectors. A contracts the wrong things: the feature dimension is what disappears, so the score matrix is T × T, never d × d; B normalizes over queries, which would make each key column sum to 1 — weights that no longer form a per-query distribution; C forgets that multiplying by V replaces the key axis with V's feature axis. Real attention divides the scores by sqrt(d) first — that changes values, never shapes.

exercise.title: Diagnose: saturation vs dead neurons
exercise.statement: A diagnosis question to finish — the kind that shows up in every deep-learning code review. Two tiny networks were trained on the same task; only their hidden activations differ. Read the observations and pick the correct diagnosis for both networks.
exercise.code:
# Two tiny MLPs, same data, same optimizer, same epochs.
#
# Net A: Dense(32, 'sigmoid') -> Dense(32, 'sigmoid')
#        -> Dense(32, 'sigmoid') -> Dense(1, 'sigmoid')
#
# Net B: Dense(32, 'relu') -> Dense(32, 'relu')
#        -> Dense(32, 'relu') -> Dense(1, 'sigmoid')
#
# Observed after training:
#   Net A: 71% of hidden activations lie within 0.02 of 0.0 or 1.0;
#          the gradient norm at hidden layer 1 is ~0.001x the norm at
#          the last hidden layer; the loss stops improving early.
#   Net B: 8 of the 32 units in hidden layer 1 output exactly 0.0 for
#          EVERY training sample, and their weights stop changing
#          after a few epochs.
options: A. Net A: exploding gradients — activations pinned at 0/1 mean the weights grew too fast. Net B: healthy sparsity; always-zero units are exactly what ReLU is designed to produce.
B. Net A: the flat loss comes from the final sigmoid alone; hidden activations near 0/1 do not affect gradients. Net B: the always-zero units have saturated at the ReLU ceiling.

C. Net A: sigmoid saturation drives vanishing gradients — near 0.0/1.0 the slope s·(1−s) is ~0, and it is at most 0.25 anywhere, so three stacked sigmoids shrink early gradients by at best 0.25³ ≈ 0.016. Net B: dead ReLU units — always-negative pre-activations give zero output and zero gradient, so those units cannot recover on their own.
D. Net A: overfitting — activations near 0 and 1 mean the network memorized the training set. Net B: underfitting, because ReLU outputs can never be negative.
exercise.explain: Check the ranges and slopes. Sigmoid lives in (0, 1) with slope s·(1−s): it peaks at 0.25 when the output is 0.5 and collapses toward 0 as the output approaches 0.0 or 1.0 — at s = 0.98 the slope is 0.98 × 0.02 ≈ 0.02. Backprop multiplies slopes, so three hidden sigmoid layers cap the layer-1 gradient at 0.25³ ≈ 0.016 of the top gradient even in the best case; with 71% of units pinned near the extremes, the products collapse to the observed ~0.001 — early layers barely learn and the loss stalls: saturation with vanishing gradients. ReLU is max(0, z): range [0, ∞), slope 1 for z > 0 and exactly 0 for z < 0. A unit that is negative for every sample outputs 0.0 always and passes zero gradient through every path — its weights and bias receive no updates: a dead neuron, matching 'weights stop changing'. A confuses vanishing with exploding (exploding shows growing gradient norms and an unstable loss); B forgets that the chain rule multiplies the hidden slopes too, and invents a 'ReLU ceiling' — ReLU is unbounded above and never saturates that way; D tells a memorization story: saturation is about gradient flow, not memory, and ReLU's non-negativity is by design.
